source.name: NASA/JPL Small-Body Database, 3200 Phaethon (1983 TB); osculating elements, equinox J2000, ecliptic plane

radius.source: JPL Small-Body Database effective diameter 6.25 km (Taylor et al. 2019, Planetary and Space Science, doi 10.1016/j.pss.2019.01.009), half of it; JPL Horizons prints RAD = 3.125 km

accuracy.statement: Position was compared with JPL Horizons at eight dates from 2020-12-14 to 2032-12-14: the largest Sun-centred difference is about 935,344 km (2.18% of its distance from the Sun at that date, 0.29 AU, 2020-12-14, close to perihelion), so this is an indicative position, good enough to show where the body is on its orbit at overview scale, not an ephemeris and not good enough for a close approach. The small perihelion distance (q about 0.14 AU) is the weak point: the body moves fastest there, so a small error in timing becomes a large error in position. Sample maximum, not a bound for every date. It was also compared at six dates across the Showers demo's year, 21 September 2019 to 20 September 2020 (Horizons solution JPL#1019, fetched 2026-10-18): the largest difference there is 365,665 km (0.16% of its distance from the Sun, 2020-09-20), within the figure above.
limitations: Horizons integrates the same orbit fit with the planets' pull and a small transverse non-gravitational term that this model leaves out, so the two drift apart.
Positions before 2019-09-21 or after 2032-12-14 were not compared with Horizons, nor any date between 2020-09-20 and 2020-12-14.
The body's size is the effective diameter of a 6 km body; no shape, spin or orientation is modelled.

source.name: NASA/JPL Small-Body Database, 3200 Phaethon (1983 TB), orbit solution of 2026-10-15 (SB441-N16, equinox J2000, osculating epoch JD 2461200.5); sizes the whole-orbit path's sampling, the asteroid's position is the two-body source built from parentElements
Global Meteor Network, monthly trajectory summary files (traj_summary_monthly_YYYYMM.txt), IAU shower 4 (GEM); Vida et al. 2021, MNRAS 506(4); Vida et al. 2020, MNRAS 491(2)

gmn.ruleNote: Qc is GMN's own maximum convergence angle between stations (column Qc, deg) and the Vgeo sigma is the uncertainty column beside Vgeo (km/s), so the reliable set is Qc at least the angle and sigma at most the fraction of Vgeo.

rule.quote: "requiring a minimum convergence angle of 15 degrees between cameras, ensuring an estimated velocity error of no more than 10% of the nominal value" (the 2025 HDBSCAN paper words it: "a minimum convergence angle of 15° between camera detections to ensure reliable triangulation, ... a velocity error not exceeding 10% of the nominal value"); both apply it to the CAMS v3.0 database; they also drop hyperbolic orbits, which the data file already does

source.name: Peña-Asensio and Sánchez-Lozano 2024, Statistical Equivalence of Metrics for Meteor Dynamical Association, Advances in Space Research, doi 10.1016/j.asr.2024.05.005 (arXiv 2405.03308); and arXiv 2507.01501, Meteoroid stream identification with HDBSCAN

concentration.basis: no clump is drawn. The Geminid stream is old and broad, and no published fraction or width of dust near Phaethon is claimed; every dot is a measured orbit spread uniformly in mean anomaly.

source.name: International Meteor Organization, 2019 Meteor Shower Calendar (ed. J. Rendtel), the Geminids entry: active December 4-17, maximum December 14, peak night December 13-14; archived copy
source.note: The peak rate is 150 meteors per hour (ZHR), the American Meteor Society calendar figure; the IMO lists 140 for 2019. The peak instant is when the Sun reaches the IAU Meteor Data Center peak solar longitude of 261.6 degrees, which falls inside the IMO's peak period. The rate curve falls off from that instant.

source.name: IAU Meteor Data Center, established meteor showers, Geminids (GEM, 4), parameter set AdNo 8 (Jenniskens 2023, Atlas of Earth's Meteor Showers): peak solar longitude 261.6 deg, geocentric radiant RA 113.0, Dec +32.4 deg, J2000
